cards.front: The term for which taste is detected, such as sweet or bitter, is {{c1::identity}}.
cards.back: A trained recognition task measures this readout in mice.
cards.quote: Identity is which taste it is: sweet, bitter, sour, salty or umami.

cards.front: What does a taste's value describe, and which behaviours measure it?
cards.back: How much the animal wants the taste: attraction or aversion, measured by approach, avoidance or licking.
cards.quote: Value is how much the animal wants it: attraction toward a taste or aversion from it, read out as approach, avoidance or licking.

cards.front: Why does increased licking for a taste fail to establish that its identity changed?
cards.back: Licking measures expressed value. Need or learning can change how much an animal wants a taste; identity requires a separate recognition measure.
cards.quote: Some of it is innate, and it changes with need and learning.

cards.front: Are taste cells neurons, and what must they signal to after detecting a chemical?
cards.back: They are not neurons; they must signal to an afferent nerve fibre.
cards.quote: A taste cell detects a chemical, but it is not a neuron, so it must hand its news to a fibre.
cards.section: Where identity starts: two cell types, two synapses

cards.front: Why is it too strong to say every mouse taste cell responds to exactly one taste quality?
cards.back: Taste-cell populations are predominantly selective, but some mouse cells respond to both sweet and umami.
cards.quote: The separation is predominant, not absolute: some mouse taste cells respond to both sweet and umami
cards.section: Where identity starts: two cell types, two synapses

cards.front: How do mouse type II and type III taste cells differ in transmitter release onto fibres?
cards.back: Type II cells release ATP through CALHM1/3 channels without a conventional vesicular synapse. Type III cells use conventional vesicular synapses and can release serotonin.
cards.quote: With no conventional vesicular synapse, the depolarized cell releases ATP through a channel
cards.section: A synapse made of a channel

cards.front: Why was the slow gating of CALHM1 alone a puzzle for ATP release by mouse type II taste cells?
cards.back: Type II cells fire brief action potentials, but CALHM1 alone activated with a time constant above 500 ms in cultured N2a cells: too slow for much opening during a brief spike.
cards.quote: A CALHM1-only gate would barely open during a brief spike.
cards.section: A synapse made of a channel

cards.front: For an illustrative first-order CALHM gate, opening approaches steady state as 1 − e^(−t/τ). During a constant 5 ms voltage step, compare τ = 500 ms with τ = 10 ms. What if τ exceeds 500 ms?
cards.back: For 500 ms: 1 − e^(−5/500) ≈ 0.00995, or 1.0%. For 10 ms: 1 − e^(−5/10) ≈ 0.393, or 39%. A time constant above 500 ms gives less opening. These are fractions of the way to steady state, not measured ATP release per spike.
cards.quote: These numbers illustrate the logic; they are not recordings, and they do not predict how much ATP leaves per spike.
cards.section: A synapse made of a channel

cards.front: Deleting Calhm3 abolishes taste-evoked ATP release from mouse taste buds; coexpressing CALHM3 with CALHM1 speeds activation in N2a cells. What do these two experiments establish together?
cards.back: CALHM3 is needed for taste-evoked release in those buds and speeds CALHM1 channel gating in cultured cells. The cell-culture time constant is not a transmission delay measured in a living mouse.
cards.quote: This is a property of cultured cells, not a delay measured in a living animal.
cards.section: A synapse made of a channel

cards.front: Mouse type III taste cells transduce acid through {{c1::OTOP1}}.
cards.back: OTOP1 is a proton channel; knockout severely attenuates acid-evoked taste-nerve responses, without necessarily abolishing them.
cards.quote: They make conventional synapses onto fibres, and they transduce acid through OTOP1.
cards.section: Type III cells, and why ATP at all

cards.front: Why does the vesicular synapse of mouse type III taste cells not imply that sour signalling is independent of ATP?
cards.back: Mice lacking both P2X2 and P2X3 lost taste-nerve responses even for qualities carried by type III cells. In the papers discussed, the cellular source of the ATP needed during sour signalling remains unresolved.
cards.quote: Which cell supplies the ATP needed during sour signalling is, so far as these papers go, still open.
cards.section: Type III cells, and why ATP at all

cards.front: In a hypothetical receptor-knockout experiment, a nerve loses taste responses but retains touch and temperature responses. What does the retained activity control for?
cards.back: It argues against complete nerve failure: the nerve still responds to other stimuli. The loss is selective for taste in the modalities tested, rather than a loss of all responsiveness.
cards.quote: while the nerves still answered touch, temperature and menthol.
cards.section: Type III cells, and why ATP at all

cards.front: A sensory coding scheme in which each taste fibre listens only to cells of one quality is a {{c1::labelled line}}.
cards.back: Activity in that fibre would indicate one taste quality.
cards.quote: If each fibre listened only to the cells of one quality, it would be a labelled line
cards.section: One quality per fibre, or one at a time

cards.front: Why would a taste fibre receiving inputs from several taste qualities require a population or timing code?
cards.back: Its activity alone is ambiguous. The brain would need the pattern across fibres or their activity timing to distinguish tastes.
cards.quote: the brain would have to read taste from the pattern across fibres or from the timing of their activity.
cards.section: One quality per fibre, or one at a time

cards.front: Which three testing choices must accompany a claim that a taste neuron is narrowly tuned?
cards.back: The stimulus panel, the concentration range and the criterion for calling a response.
cards.quote: the stimulus panel, the concentration range and the criterion for calling a response.
cards.section: One quality per fibre, or one at a time

cards.front: Mouse bitter-sour geniculate neurons retain both responses after PKD2L1-marked sour cells are silenced, while sour-only responses disappear. Which input hypothesis does this support, and why does the sour-only control matter?
cards.back: It supports input from bitter cells that acid also activates. Convergent sour-cell input predicts loss of the acid response. Disappearance of sour-only responses checks that sour-cell silencing worked.
cards.quote: convergence predicted the loss of these neurons' acid response, and the class survived.
cards.section: One quality per fibre, or one at a time

cards.front: Why does disappearance of the mouse bitter-sour neuron class after blocking bitter responses fail to distinguish convergence from acid activation of bitter cells?
cards.back: Both hypotheses predict loss of the bitter-sour class. The result establishes dependence on bitter signalling, but does not distinguish the source of its acid response.
cards.quote: The second column does not separate the ideas, because both predict it; it confirms that the class depends on bitter signalling.
cards.section: One quality per fibre, or one at a time

cards.front: In a made-up taste-neuron model, inputs have weights 1 and 0.4; both activate to 0.33 at low concentration and 0.89 at high concentration. A response must exceed 0.25. At which concentration does the neuron respond to both tastes?
cards.back: Only at high concentration. Low: main input = 1 × 0.33 = 0.33; weak input = 0.4 × 0.33 = 0.132, below 0.25. High: main input = 1 × 0.89 = 0.89; weak input = 0.4 × 0.89 = 0.356, above 0.25. Fixed wiring can therefore look broader at higher strength.
cards.quote: Nothing about this neuron's wiring changed; the stimulus did, measured against a fixed threshold.
cards.section: One quality per fibre, or one at a time

cards.front: A model taste neuron's weak input has weight 0.2, activation saturates at 1, and responses must exceed 0.25. Can increasing concentration make that weak input count as a response, and why?
cards.back: No. Even at full activation, the input contributes only 0.2, below 0.25. Some model neurons can remain singly responsive despite increasing concentration.
cards.quote: That input never crosses the threshold: even at full activation it contributes only 0.2, below 0.25.
cards.section: One quality per fibre, or one at a time

cards.front: A taste-neuron model broadens with concentration under a fixed absolute response threshold. Now count responses using a fixed fraction of each neuron's best response, with all inputs scaling identically with concentration. What happens to breadth, and why?
cards.back: Breadth stays constant under the relative criterion because each input keeps the same fraction of the best response. This rests on the rules that tuning depends on the response criterion and that identical concentration scaling preserves input ratios; broadening under an absolute threshold need not imply changed wiring.
cards.quote: Suppose a response were instead counted relative to the neuron's own best response, and every input rose with concentration in the same way.
cards.section: One quality per fibre, or one at a time

cards.front: Separate mouse geniculate cohorts contain 28 multiply responsive neurons out of 101 at a low-concentration panel and 79 out of 155 at a mid-range panel. Calculate each percentage. Does this establish broadening of individual neurons?
cards.back: Low: 100 × 28/101 ≈ 27.7%. Mid-range: 100 × 79/155 ≈ 51.0%. The sampled population looks broader, but separate cohorts cannot establish that any individual neuron broadened.
cards.quote: The arithmetic shows that the population looked broader, not that any single neuron broadened
cards.section: One quality per fibre, or one at a time

cards.front: Design a taste-neuron study that distinguishes concentration-dependent broadening within cells from differences between sampled cohorts, while avoiding treating many cells from one animal as independent animal replicates.
cards.back: Track the same neurons at both concentrations with a matched stimulus panel and response criterion, across multiple animals. Report paired cell changes within animals and their consistency across animals. This follows the rules that cohort fractions cannot show individual change and that cells from a few animals are not independent replicates.
cards.quote: Only a within-neuron comparison at low and high concentration tests that
cards.section: One quality per fibre, or one at a time

cards.front: A cortical map ordered by taste quality is called {{c1::gustotopic}}.
cards.back: Separate fields were reported in sampled regions of anaesthetized mouse cortex; a fixed map remains disputed.
cards.quote: That is a gustotopic (taste-quality-ordered) map, in anaesthetized mice, within the regions sampled
cards.section: What cortex does with a taste

cards.front: How should separate cortical taste fields in anaesthetized mice be reconciled with distributed responses in alert, licking mice?
cards.back: Interpret each result within its state and sampling. The evidence does not settle a fixed map; sampling matters as well as anaesthesia versus alertness.
cards.quote: The two results differ in state and sampling, so they do not simply contradict each other
cards.section: What cortex does with a taste

cards.front: In awake mice, driving sweet or bitter cortical fields evokes attraction or aversion; blocking a field impairs recognition of its taste, which recovers on washout. What sufficiency and necessity claims follow?
cards.back: Driving the fields is sufficient for attraction or aversion in these assays; field activity is needed for recognition in the trained task. This does not establish subjective sweetness or cortex as the only taste representation.
cards.quote: So the driven fields were sufficient for attraction or aversion, and needed for recognition in this task.
cards.section: What cortex does with a taste

cards.front: Why train taste recognition with bitter as go and sweet as no-go, and what alternative strategy can still solve this reversed mapping?
cards.back: It prevents responding from simply following attraction. But an animal could still learn to respond to the unpleasant taste, so reversed mapping alone does not isolate identity.
cards.quote: a mouse could learn the rule "respond to the unpleasant one".
cards.section: What cortex does with a taste

cards.front: In a hypothetical recognition task, both an attractive low-salt stimulus and an aversive bitter stimulus require go responses. Why is success evidence against solving the task by liking alone?
cards.back: Go responses span opposite values, so an attraction-versus-aversion rule cannot separate go from no-go. This constrains a value-only strategy without proving a particular subjective taste experience.
cards.quote: low salt, which mice find attractive, shared the go branch with bitter, so liking alone could not solve the task.
cards.section: What cortex does with a taste

cards.front: What let researchers activate mouse sweet or bitter cortical fields with light?
cards.back: Expression of channelrhodopsin, a light-gated ion channel, in the targeted cortical field.
cards.quote: expressed channelrhodopsin, a light-gated ion channel, in the sweet or bitter field in awake mice.
cards.section: What cortex does with a taste

cards.front: Which two behavioural readouts dissociated when the amygdala was silenced in the mouse taste experiments?
cards.back: Attraction elicited by sweet-cortex stimulation disappeared, while trained sweet-versus-bitter recognition remained correct.
cards.quote: the attraction elicited by stimulating sweet cortex was abolished, while the mice still reported sweet and bitter correctly in the trained recognition tasks.
cards.section: Identity and value can be pulled apart

cards.front: Does loss of sweet-cortex-driven attraction after mouse amygdala silencing establish that all taste value is first computed in the amygdala? Use another observation to assess the claim.
cards.back: No. The silencing dissociates two readouts in those assays; it does not locate the first value computation. Decerebrate rats still accept sweet and reject bitter in taste-reactivity tests. The reasoning rests on assay-limited necessity and the rule that brainstem circuits can support innate acceptance and rejection.
cards.quote: Read that at its scope: these assays and this silencing method.
cards.section: Identity and value can be pulled apart

cards.front: What is sodium appetite's behavioural signature after sodium depletion?
cards.back: The animal drinks salt concentrations it would normally reject.
cards.quote: a sodium-depleted animal drinks salt concentrations it would normally reject.
cards.section: Value that moves with need

cards.front: Why does sodium depletion increasing salt intake establish a change in expressed value without proving an unchanged taste signal?
cards.back: Intake shows increased wanting. The same salt can evoke different behaviour, but behaviour alone does not measure whether its taste signal or identity also changed.
cards.quote: Behaviour alone does not show that the salt's taste signal is unchanged.
cards.section: Value that moves with need

cards.front: In sodium-depleted mice, oral salt rapidly suppresses recorded sodium-appetite neurons, whereas gastric NaCl infusion does not in the same acute window. What temporal conclusion follows, and what remains possible?
cards.back: Oral contact can suppress activity faster than the gastric route in that comparison. Slower feedback from the gut remains possible; the acute negative result does not exclude it.
cards.quote: The gastric comparison covers only a short window and does not exclude slower feedback from the gut.
cards.section: Value that moves with need

cards.front: The mouse gut-to-brain circuit studied in the lesson is silenced. What happens to the development of sugar preference, and why does this caution against explaining wanting solely from tongue chemistry?
cards.back: Development of sugar preference was prevented in that experiment. Wanting can depend on signals beyond the tongue; this result does not itself establish a changed taste identity.
cards.quote: silencing a gut-to-brain circuit in mice prevented the development of sugar preference
cards.section: Value that moves with need

cards.front: A drug reduces sucrose intake. Design a within-animal comparison that tests whether expressed value changes while trained identity recognition is spared. How would you interpret intact recognition with reduced sucrose licking?
cards.back: Compare drug with vehicle within animals. Separately measure brief-access sucrose licking and recognition in a task where attractive low salt shares the go response with bitter, so liking alone cannot solve it. Intact recognition with reduced licking is consistent with altered expressed value in these assays. This uses the rule that identity and value need separate readouts; it does not locate the drug's action or establish subjective experience.
cards.quote: Give the drug and vehicle to the same animals, so each mouse is its own control.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A drug weakens taste signals without necessarily changing taste quality. What recognition pattern could appear as sucrose concentration rises, and why?
cards.back: Recognition could fail at low concentrations but recover at high ones, because stronger stimulation can make a weakened signal sufficient for detection and task performance. Low-concentration failure alone does not establish changed identity.
cards.quote: A drug that weakens the signal might impair recognition at low concentrations and spare it at high ones
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A drug impairs sweet-versus-bitter recognition but spares a matched two-tone go/no-go task. Which taste tests would constrain detection loss versus changed quality, and what does the tone control leave unresolved?
cards.back: Test sucrose-versus-water detection across concentrations, quality discrimination with concentration varied to prevent intensity cues, and trial omissions. The tone control checks some general task deficits but cannot separate taste-detection loss from changed quality. This follows the rule that failed recognition can reflect detection, attention, motivation or responding, not uniquely identity.
cards.quote: it cannot tell a taste-detection deficit from a changed taste quality.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why measure licking for water when a drug reduces licking for sucrose?
cards.back: To check whether the drug reduces licking generally. Reduced water licking would weaken an interpretation specific to sucrose value.
cards.quote: check that the drug does not simply reduce licking for everything, by testing licking for water.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why do mitochondria beside mouse type II taste-cell CALHM1 patches not by themselves prove that mitochondria supply the released ATP?
cards.back: Images establish geometry, not ATP's source. Oligomycin eliminating depolarization-evoked ATP release supplies indirect pharmacological support for a mitochondrial source.
cards.quote: The images show geometry. The case for a mitochondrial ATP source rests on indirect pharmacology
cards.section: Microscopy and mitochondria

cards.front: Two mouse studies disagree on whether activating acid-sensing taste cells drives licking when no water is delivered. Design a comparison to test driver-population and thirst-state explanations, and state the limit of a positive result.
cards.back: Compare driver/reporter lines side by side, count targeted cells and match light settings. Test water deprivation, food deprivation, salt depletion and repletion, measuring licking versus water within animals. Confirm nerve activation after behaviour. If licking appears only during thirst, activation can direct licking in thirsty mice. This rests on matched targeting and state controls; light supplies no water, so licking cannot establish rehydration.
cards.quote: The two results may differ because different cells were reached.
cards.section: A disputed thirst experiment
